Kroizer pointed out that MKs from both parties walked out of the plenum during the singing of "Hatikvah," Israel's national anthem, as part of the Knesset's swearing-in ceremony last week. "It is a slap in the face to the fallen soldiers of the Israel Defense Forces, the victims of terror, and those currently serving in the IDF," he said, adding that lawmakers who "glorify 'martyrs'" and refuse to condemn the Hamas terror group are now "playing a decisive role" in the Knesset. Kroizer called Kahana, a former Israeli Air Force pilot who served as religious services minister under then-Prime Minister Naftali Bennett in 2021 and 2022, "a worthy individual who has contributed greatly to the state." However, the speaker was elected with the votes of "Tibi, Abbas, and their associates," Kroizer said. He noted the Arab lawmakers had dedicated their gains in the Oct. 27 election to "their 'brothers,' the Nukhba terrorists in Gaza." "This badge of shame will remain with him forever," Kroizer said. "It must be clear to the public that these parties do not seek the well-being of Israel's citizens; rather, time and again, they align themselves with those who seek our destruction," he added. The plenum approved a recommendation by the temporary Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, following a government request. The declaration is usually renewed for a year, but the temporary committee formed after the Oct. 27 Knesset election can only approve four-month extensions, Hebrew media reported. The declaration has been in effect since the Jewish state's founding in 1948, when the Provisional State Council issued it. It lets the government enact emergency regulations that can override Knesset legislation, subject to legal limits. It also keeps certain laws and orders that depend on the emergency in force.

From Gaza ceasefire negotiations to U.S.-Israel relations and from Iran’s nuclear ambitions to the war on terror, Blum and Regev dissect the week’s headlines with authority, candor and a touch of humor. What sets “Israel Undiplomatic” apart is the dynamic between its hosts: Two seasoned insiders often agree on the goals but clash on the details. title: A century of hope: How global medical breakthroughs shape the future of healthcare
description: Imagine being told you will never walk again, and then, through sheer resilience and world-class care, taking your very first steps. Imagine waiting for a lifesaving medical treatment that does not yet exist, only to benefit from a pioneering discovery that completely rewrites your future. Every day at Hadassah hospitals in Jerusalem, these inspiring stories unfold. Behind every outcome is a dedicated team of physicians, researchers and innovators pushing the boundaries of medicine. From complex, groundbreaking surgeries to vital advances in treatments for diseases affecting people across the globe, the impact extends far beyond borders. Hadassah, The Women’s Zionist Organization of America , powers the work of the hospitals through the collective strength of 300,000 members, Associates and supporters. It is a life-changing force for those who heal and for those who help make that healing possible. An international impact driven by research and care The scale of care delivered at Hadassah hospitals is immense. Each year, the organization serves more than 1 million patients, touching the lives of 1 in 10 Israelis. In 2025 alone, Hadassah hospitals welcomed 19,007 newborns into the world; performed 51,882 surgeries with precision care; launched nearly 2,000 clinical trials; and were awarded 25 new patents. The cutting-edge care is transformational. Take the story of Jonathan, a father of three who suffered severe, life-threatening trauma following a major highway accident. Transferred directly to the Level 1 trauma center at Hadassah Hospital Ein Kerem, his survival depended on an intricate, multistage surgical intervention led by an interdisciplinary team. Today, he is back home with his family, which is a testament to the hospital’s world-renowned emergency response and medical ingenuity. Whether pioneering research in cancer, ALS, Alzheimer’s disease or trauma medicine, Hadassah hospitals serve as a crucial bridge to peace, modeling a shared society through interfaith cooperation in daily clinical care and international medical collaboration. When terror, natural disasters or healthcare crises strike, Hadassah is on the frontlines. In the United States, Hadassah does more than support the compassionate care and research at its hospitals; it unites generations of women and families in purpose. Through dedicated support for Youth Aliyah Villages , Hadassah provides shelter, education, counseling, compassion and essential life skills to vulnerable teens and pre-teens in Israel, helping over 300,000 graduates build bright futures since 1934. At a time when the Jewish state and the global Jewish community face extraordinary challenges, Hadassah remains nonpartisan, advocating for women’s health equity; speaking out against hate and antisemitism; and championing a strong and secure Israel. Driven by a movement of women changemakers, the organization gives individuals the tools to lead, connect and create impact. At Hadassah, we believe that each of us has the potential to make a difference. How to get involved Healing the world takes action. There are ways to make an enduring impact: •       Become a member : Join a national network of nearly 300,000 women and advocates standing together for Israel and women's health. •       Support lifesaving research : Donate to fund pioneering medical research and state-of-the-art facilities and equipment at Hadassah hospitals. •       Advocate for change : Participate in national campaigns fighting antisemitism and anti-Zionism and advancing women’s health. Learn how you can be part of this legacy of hope and healing by exploring Our Impact . Visit: Hadassah.org .

title: Sotheby’s reaches deal with Jewish heirs over $180 million Van Gogh
description: Sotheby’s auction house announced on Wednesday that it had reached an agreement with the heirs of a German Jewish publisher over the contested sale of a Vincent van Gogh painting his family had sold in Amsterdam after the Nazis rose to power in Germany. “In recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement,” Sotheby’s said in a statement , referring to the Fischer heirs and the painting's current owners. The agreement with the heirs of publisher Samuel Fischer concerned the “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (“Chestnut Trees in Blossom”), which is to be auctioned in New York on Wednesday and whose worth was estimated at $180 million. The terms of the agreement were not disclosed. The U.S.-based heirs, who had asked Sotheby’s to freeze the sale, said the 1890 work was sold in Amsterdam in 1936 because of financial losses their family’s publishing company suffered under Nazi rule. The Netherlands was not then under Nazi control, but the heirs argue that persecution in Germany forced the sale.

title: Revolt-era hideouts and Byzantine church open to visitors in Judean Foothills
description: Tunnels where Jewish rebels sheltered some 2,000 years ago, alongside a Byzantine church paved with colorful mosaics, opened to the public this past weekend at Horvat Burgin in Adullam–France Park. The inauguration was a joint effort of KKL-JNF, the Israel Antiquities Authority and the Mateh Yehuda Regional Council, capping years of excavation, conservation and development. Digs led by Dr. Amir Ganor, Alon Klein and Dr. Peter Gendelman uncovered a settlement that endured from the Second Temple period through Ottoman times. Researchers suggest the large Second Temple village may be Caphar Bish, a place named by the historian Flavius Josephus. As tensions with Rome mounted in the Early Roman period, residents carved sprawling hiding networks into the bedrock. The settlement was destroyed during the Bar Kokhba Revolt of 132–136 CE. A pagan population later moved into the ruins, building anew above ground and cutting elaborate burial complexes beneath. In the Byzantine era, a church and monastery rose on the site. Dovecotes and winepresses found in the vicinity show that residents made their living from pigeon breeding, farming and winemaking. Ganor, who heads the Antiquities Authority’s Antiquities Theft Prevention Unit, described Horvat Burgin as the area’s largest ancient settlement. For years, he said, looters ravaged burial caves and tunnels and damaged standing structures. Enforcement operations, arrests of looting gangs, rescue excavations and the park’s opening finally stopped the destruction. “The site was saved,” Ganor said, “and now it can be enjoyed by the public.”

She said first responders had been trying to save lives "under unimaginable conditions." "Chaotic scenes, fragmented evidence and the absence of forensic evidence are often the starting point," Israeli-Amarant explained. Establishing the facts, she added, requires "painstaking work and honesty about what remains unknown." She called for a wider view than rape alone. Guidelines must be developed with first responders, Israeli-Amarant said. "Their physical safety and emotional well-being must be central. The Peruvian delegation included senior officers from national security agencies, counterterrorism experts and government representatives. Seventeen Israeli defense companies presented technologies tailored to the operational needs identified by Peru’s security agencies, including cybersecurity, drones and counter-drone systems, secure communications, VIP protection, intelligence gathering, big data and artificial intelligence. Participating companies included Robotican, Steadicopter, Roboteam, Rayzone Group, D-Fend Solutions and Netline Communications Technologies. Authorities had run a covert investigation for several weeks after receiving indications that drones bought from the suspect had been used for crimes. The seized drones had "various tactical capabilities," according to the statement. Customs officials from Ben-Gurion International Airport questioned the suspect over serious customs offenses and regulatory violations in communications and aviation. He was then handed to police for questioning on suspicion of conspiracy to commit a crime.

"On one hand, there is a heavy sense of responsibility," Shalev said. "I am here on behalf of my comrades who saved the country: those who are still with us, those who were wounded and those who are no longer here." "Naturally, there is also a great deal of excitement and new experiences, but above all, there is a desire to shape the future for the younger generation in Israel," he said. "The issues I wish to advance concern those who serve, ensuring that those who sacrifice so much are placed at the very top of the state's list of priorities," Shalev said. He also pledged that in every decision, "the interests of the younger generation, those who will live here for many decades to come, are taken into account."

title: Netanyahu's office slams Eisenkot letter as politicizing security
description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office on Wednesday accused Yashar chief Gadi Eisenkot of politicizing national security, after the leader of the opposition bloc sent a letter urging him to avoid "dangerous moves" while a new government is being formed. The Prime Minister's Office called the missive "an irresponsible move to publicly discuss sensitive security issues." It said all decisions were made "solely out of security considerations" and "in full coordination with the security establishment." It added that Netanyahu "once again calls on Gadi Eisenkot to join the government that is fighting terrorism," rather than "trying to form a government with supporters of terrorism," in a reference to the opposition bloc's ongoing negotiations with Arab lawmakers. In his letter, Eisenkot had cited "very worrying reports" in recent weeks about "extraneous considerations" entering "the holy of holies: Israel's security." "I demand of you: In this sensitive period, you are required to show national responsibility," the missive said. Eisenkot urged "restraint and caution regarding dangerous moves that can wait for the swearing-in of a new government that wins the Knesset's confidence."

Everyone should be able to enter a place of worship without fear.” Unia, Belgium’s equality body, received 192 reports of antisemitism in 2025. That was down from 277 in 2024 but up from 121 in 2023. title: Hebrew University of Jerusalem presents honorary fellowship to philanthropist Dr. Wallace Weber
description: The Hebrew University of Jerusalem presented an honorary fellowship to Dr. Wallace Weber during its 89th Board of Governors Meeting on Oct. 19 in Jerusalem. Weber is a retired dermatologist whose specialty practice expanded to include several offices throughout Kansas. He previously served in the Gulf War as a flight surgeon with the 82nd Airborne Division, later commanding the 410th U.S. Army Reserve Evacuation Hospital in Topeka. He retired from the U.S. Army after 31 years of service with awards including the Southwest Asia Service Medal and the Legion of Merit. Weber supports scholarships and regenerative agriculture at the Hebrew University's Robert H. Smith Faculty of Agriculture, Food and Environment, as well as other initiatives. He held a volunteer faculty appointment within the dermatology division at the University of Kansas School of Medicine, where he also created and endowed the university's annual lectureship, Military and Catastrophic Medicine. Weber was commissioned as a second lieutenant through the ROTC program at Colorado State University in 1965. He earned his medical degree from the University of Kansas School of Medicine in 1969. Professor Tamir Sheafer, president of the Hebrew University, bestowed the fellowship with the following citation: "in recognition of his long-standing support of Israel and the Hebrew University; in acknowledgement of his deep commitment to agricultural research and regenerative agriculture; in appreciation of his contribution to a safer world through many years of military service; in esteem for his remarkable career as a medical doctor and as an academic; in praise of his tireless efforts on behalf of the Hebrew University in the United States; and in deep gratitude for his generous donations to student scholarships and water research at the Hebrew University’s Robert H. Smith Faculty of Agriculture, Food and Environment." In accepting the honor, Weber stated, “It is an incredible and unexpected honor to be recognized by such a prestigious institution of higher learning as the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. It is with much satisfaction and fondness for the accomplished members and staff of AFHU, as well as the staff, faculty and administration of the Jerusalem and Rehovot facilities, that I can reflect on my support journey over several decades.” Weber added, “It all started with a suggestion by one of the members of AFHU. The warmth and enthusiasm demonstrated in the initial contact with Beth McCoy [AFHU’s previous CEO] will ever be fond in my memory. Her staff’s ever-present willingness to help problem-solve and make me feel valued as a member of AFHU plays a major role in my support of this institution.”

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc won 53 seats in the Oct. 27 Knesset election. The Zionist opposition parties—Yashar, B’Yachad (Together), The Democrats and Yisrael Beiteinu—won 48. The Arab Joint List and Ra’am together secured 19 seats, leaving neither bloc with the 61 seats needed for a Knesset majority. Eisenkot said he was working to form “a national emergency government” as soon as possible. He vowed to strengthen the “bipartisan foundations” of U.S.-Israel ties, adding that Jerusalem would remain “one of America’s most reliable and capable strategic partners in the Middle East.” Eisenkot said he looks forward to working “closely and constructively” with U.S. President Donald Trump and his administration. In his Oct. 18 endorsement , Trump explicitly linked further American action against Iran to Netanyahu’s re-election. “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” he wrote. To all our friends in the United States and around the world: The Israeli people have voted for change and to replace the current government. Our democracy remains strong and vibrant. Each ballot is sealed in a second envelope bearing the voter's details. Election officials use this to confirm that no one voted twice. The inner envelopes are then removed and mixed together to protect ballot secrecy. They are counted at a facility in the Knesset parking garage. title: Irish man gets suspended sentence for threatening Jews in France
description: An Irish man was handed a suspended sentence of six months in prison for threatening to kill a Jewish person near Marseille in August, French media reported on Tuesday. The man, identified in La Provence and other French media as Patrick O’Brien, 60, was filmed in Avignon in August telling an Australian Jewish couple that he regretted Adolf Hitler had not “finished the job,” expressing hope for Hitler's return and threatening to shoot the woman in the head. He admitted intending to hurt the couple verbally after realizing that the man was Jewish. In court, he described himself as a “great humanist,” La Provence said. The Avignon court convicted him of glorifying crimes against humanity and making death threats aggravated by antisemitic prejudice. He was ordered to pay €500 ($556) to each victim and €300 ($333) to several civil-party organizations. The court rejected prosecutors' request to ban him from French territory for three years. A lawyer representing the victims, Annie Cohen, said the sentence was excessively lenient, La Provence reported, noting that the woman's father was a Holocaust survivor. The incident had attracted widespread attention in France after a video of the confrontation went viral in August.

NPO chairwoman Jet de Ranitz said discussions with broadcasters had initially suggested that a Dutch entry was possible, but efforts to reach an agreement had failed. “Because of the sensitivities surrounding the issues currently at play, we have decided to take a step back,” she said, according to NOS , a major news broadcaster affiliated with NPO. The decision followed criticism of Israel’s military operations in Gaza. Several European broadcasters have called for Israel’s exclusion. In August, Dutch broadcaster AVROTROS announced it would boycott Eurovision for a second consecutive year, arguing that the competition could no longer be considered politically neutral. NPO said it would look into tasking a different broadcaster with organizing Dutch official participation in the event. However, the plan encountered significant resistance within the NPO's constituent bodies. Earlier this month, more than 400 NPO employees signed a letter protesting participation alongside Israel. The European Broadcasting Union, which organizes Eurovision, expressed regret over the Dutch decision but said it respected the broadcaster’s position, NOS reported. Ireland has also announced that it will boycott Eurovision in 2027, citing the humanitarian situation in Gaza. Unlike the Netherlands, Ireland will not broadcast the event. Israel finished second at the 2026 Eurovision Song Contest in Vienna, which was won by Bulgaria’s Dara.

Nouman Essghir, also 24, was charged with entering a prohibited location for a purpose harmful to British national security. Both men were scheduled to appear in court on Tuesday. description: A former insurance executive in Ireland’s branch of the AIG firm who said his social media account had been hacked and used to vilify Jews is no longer with the company, his former boss recently told local Jews last week. AIG Ireland’s president and chief executive, Eric Andersen, informed the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland (JRCI) in an email of his firm’s parting of ways with John Gillick, former head of consumer marketing and sponsorship, The Irish Times reported on Sunday. Under Gillick’s account on X, text appeared last month that described Israel and Jews as “human scum” and Jews as “filthy dogs,” according to the report. One post stated: “Jews in Ireland need to be thrown out. They are traitors and land thieves. Our children need to be educated more about how evil Israel and Jews are,” and, “no one should associate with murdering jew war criminals.” On Sept. 2, a post on the account read: “I want to let people know that my account has been compromised by unauthorised person(s) and that recent posts containing anti-Semitic content were not written, published or endorsed by me,” and, “I unequivocally condemn the views expressed in those posts. They do not reflect my beliefs or values. I strongly oppose discrimination and hate in all forms.” Initially, AIG Ireland said the social media posts in question were “fraudulently published following the unauthorised compromise of an employee’s personal social media account.” However, in informing JCRI of Gillick’s departure, Andersen wrote that matter of the posts was the subject of an ongoing police investigation, and an internal one at AIG Ireland. JRCI Chair Orli Degani told The Irish Times that she did not know the circumstances surrounding Gillick’s departure, but welcomed AIG’s investigation, the newspaper reported.

title: Jewish Choral Conducting Institute graduates first cohort of fellows
description: The Jewish Choral Conducting Institute (JCCI), a program dedicated to high-level training of conductors of Jewish choral music, has graduated its first cohort of fellows. JCCI was created by Maestro Matthew Lazar, founder and director of the Zamir Choral Foundation, to provide professional education and pass on the tradition and experience of Jewish choral music to the next generation. The fully funded institute is made possible by a major gift from Cantor Robert Lieberman and Rabbi Vicki Lieberman. Each JCCI cohort is composed of 11-15 conducting students from around the world. During the immersive two-year program, fellows attend intensive in-person retreats, workshops and monthly online meetings and receive one-on-one mentoring sessions with Lazar and guest presenters. Lazar brings knowledge of Jewish and Western music and a deep understanding of the relationship between text and music that defines choral music. He models, encourages and nurtures the talents of a new generation of conductors of Jewish music. "The conductor integrates music, text and cultural identity with mastery and precision, creating inspiring and transformative musical moments," Lazar said. "The institute provides the specialized skills and knowledge needed to make all this possible." The inaugural group of fellows has completed the program. They were presented with a certificate in Jewish Choral Conducting and performed in a recital at the North American Jewish Choral Festival. The graduates are Shani Chamovitz, Abram Foster, Joshua Gonzalez, Matthew Gonzalez, Joel Herman, Dor Kaminka, Juliana Rappaport, Elliot Roman, Yoel Rubinstein, Nitzan Shohaam and Hadas Sturman. A new cohort of JCCI fellows recently began the program, continuing the mission to share the legacy of Jewish choral music with the next generation. "We are guided by a vision of vibrant Jewish identity through the study and performance of Jewish music at the highest level of excellence. Our goal is to create a pipeline of talented and knowledgeable conductors of Jewish choral music who will ensure the future of this rich and empowering art form," Lazar said. For more information, visit: www.zamirchoralfoundation.org .

title: Italy arrests Hamas advocate over street riots
description: Authorities in Italy last week arrested a 30-year-old academic who justified Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, massacres for allegedly organizing violent demonstrations in Milan inspired by riots in France. Youssef Siher is suspected of inciting violence for terrorist purposes, Corriere della Sera reported on Saturday. A dual citizen of Italy and Morocco, Siher was the administrator of the Instagram page “Movimento 17 Ottobre” ("October 17 Movement"), which called for demonstrations across Italy. Siher, an organizer of Palestinian anti-Israel actions of Italy, in a 2024 essay defended the Hamas-led terrorist attacks in southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, the report said. He wrote in the magazine Miccia : "Few in the West were able to conceive without ifs and buts of ‘Operation Al-Aqsa Flood’ for what it was: a revolutionary act of decolonization.” "Operation Al-Aqsa Flood" is the name that Hamas gave its rampage, in which terrorists killed some 1,200 people and abducted 251 others, amid other war crimes.   Siher had no criminal record before his arrest, the report said. His wife is under investigation on suspicion of the same offenses attributed to him. The Milan clashes are part of the apparent spread of rioting that began in France several weeks ago. Italian authorities have detained more than 370 people over the weekend and arrested nine in connection with the riots, in which far-left agitators have taken to the streets along with other protesters, many of African and Middle Eastern descent, to protest a diverse range of issues, from underfunding of education to racism in society. Similar protests have begun to occur in Spain, where authorities in Barcelona detained more than 100 people over the weekend.

The bishop of Blackburn, Philip North, was among the prominent officials who condemned the incident, which police are investigating as a hate crime, the report said.
